main.faq1Q: What are SEO, AEO, and GEO?
main.faq1A: SEO (search engine optimization) is the fundamentals for being found on traditional search engines like Google. AEO (answer engine optimization) is about whether AI answer engines like ChatGPT or Perplexity can cite this page in their answers. GEO (generative engine optimization) is about whether generative AI can accurately understand and cite your content. meta-scan checks all three, each as its own checklist group.
main.faq2A: Yes — meta-scan is completely free, with no signup or payment required.
main.faq3A: SEO — basic tags (title, description, image alt), indexing (sitemap, canonical, noindex), and previews (OG, Twitter cards). AEO・GEO — the AI Signals card checks structured data, prompts.txt, an FAQ section, and how much the page depends on JS rendering. On top of that, content quality (word count, heading structure) and internationalization/UX (hreflang, viewport) round out 6 groups total, each item judged pass・warning・fail・info.
main.faq4Q: What files do I need for AEO・GEO?
main.faq4A: Nothing is required, but adding prompts.txt and a PromptObject makes it easier for AI answer engines to cite your page. Both are info-level signals — missing either isn't a deduction, just a suggestion.
main.faq5A: robots.txt is checked first, then the sitemap, page crawl, and Lighthouse run in sequence — usually around 30 seconds to a minute, depending on the site's size and response speed.
main.faq6A: No. Scan results are currently processed statelessly and aren't written to a database — each scan is only visible on that results screen.
main.faqCtaText: Still have questions? Run the SEO・AEO・GEO checklist on your site.
main.checkGroup1Body: Presence and length of the title and meta description, and image alt coverage: the basics that decide how you look in search results.
main.checkGroup2Body: Whether robots.txt blocks crawlers, whether sitemap.xml exists, and whether canonical and noindex are set as intended. The first place to look if you don't show up at all.
main.checkGroup3Body: Open Graph and Twitter card tags and og:image size, which build the card people see when your link is shared in chat apps and social feeds.
main.checkGroup4Body: Whether AI search like ChatGPT and Perplexity can read and cite the page: structured data (JSON-LD), FAQ, AI guidance files and JavaScript rendering dependence.
main.checkGroup5Body: Body length and heading structure: the skeleton people and search engines need to understand what the page is about.
main.checkGroup6Body: For multilingual sites, whether hreflang links language versions, and whether a viewport is set so the page works on mobile.
main.checkGroup7Body: Google's own Performance, SEO, Accessibility and Best Practices scores, with its improvement suggestions as-is.

sections.heading: Who builds it
body: I'm a frontend developer. At a previous job I improved a product using SEO work and Lighthouse metrics as the yardstick, and grew its MAU by 350%.
The lesson was that fundamentals come before tricks: crawlers not blocked, a unique title and description on every page, link previews that actually render, and Lighthouse issues fixed one by one.

sections.heading: Why it exists
body: Back then I checked all of this by hand, hopping between dev tools and a handful of websites. Seeing it in one place would have been much faster, so I built META_SCAN.
People now ask ChatGPT or Perplexity before they search Google. So on top of classic SEO checks, META_SCAN also checks AEO/GEO signals: whether AI can read and cite your page.

sections.heading: What's different
body: No single blended score. Each check is pass, warning, fail or info, so you know what to fix first. The only numeric scores are Google's own four Lighthouse scores, shown as-is.
It's free with no sign-up, and scan results aren't stored on the server. The blog explains why each check matters and how to fix it.
